Photograph: Courtesy Robert Hickman Missouri Suspect in shooting death of teen on Missouri highway charged in second road incident Man accused of shooting teen, who was driving to a party, has also been linked to shooting of a vehicle days earlier Jessica Glenza Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.16 EDT Last modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man accused in the shooting death of a Missouri teen has been charged in a second shooting incident – both of which involve firing into cars on the highway. Alyssa Wilson, 17, was shot and killed as she drove down Interstate 170 in Overland, Missouri, on 14 October. The teen was on her way to a Halloween party at St Louis Zoo, called Boo at the Zoo, when a suspect fired a single shot into the back of Wilson’s Buick Encore. The shot struck Wilson in the back, incapacitated her, and sent her crashing into a concrete highway median, according to prosecutors. She was pronounced dead at Barnes-Jewish Hospital. The suspected shooter, Willie James Herndon, 43, of Texas, had no known relationship to the teen. “Alyssa was 17, excited about her life, excited about her future,” her father Robert Hickman said, as state charges were announced . “She had 60 days until she turned 18, and we were getting ready to take our first family vacation together to go to Disney for her to see her favorite person in the world, Princess Tiana, and unfortunately, she’s not going to get to do that any more. This was a senseless act.” Now, federal court documents show that Herndon has been charged in a second shooting incident, this one just a few days earlier. On 11 October, St Louis metropolitan police received a report that a vehicle was shot just after exiting Interstate 55 in Missouri. Surveillance footage captured a white SUV fleeing the scene – a vehicle that matched the appearance of Herndon’s Buick Enclave. A shell casing was also recovered from the scene. Prosecutors said they were conducting ballistics tests to determine if it was fired from the same weapon that killed Wilson. In a federal criminal complaint, prosecutors lay out how they tracked what appeared to be Herndon’s Buick Enclave from the first shooting incident on 11 October, then the scene of Wilson’s death on 14 October, to a Days Inn in Caseyville, Illinois 16 October. There, prosecutors approached Herndon’s wife Taiya Herndon, 45, and were speaking to her when Herndon “emerged” from the hotel room and began to flee. As he was arrested, he was “screaming words about a shooting”, prosecutors said. Inside the Days Inn hotel room, prosecutors said they found a ABC-15 rifle “in plain view”, ammunition that matched the kind used in Wilson’s shooting, a receipt from a gas station near the scene of Wilson’s death on Interstate 170, two license plates and handwritten notes describing police vehicles Herndon believed were tracking him. Federal prosecutors in Illinois have charged Herndon with being a felon in possession of a firearm. He has separately been charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action in St Louis county, Missouri. His federal public defender did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPIMage/AP Helen Haines Helen Haines’s first words after alleged attack were about safety of staff and gratitude to bystanders, MP reveals Allegra Spender calls Indi MP ‘force for change’ as politicians pay tribute in parliament Follow our Australian politics live blog for latest updates Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Sun 25 Oct 2026 22.05 EDT First published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 20.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Helen Haines’s first words after an alleged attack last week were to ask about the safety of her staff and express gratitude to bystanders and doctors. Allegra Spender, the MP for Wentworth, told parliament on Monday that Haines’s husband, Phil Haines, had revealed the Indi MP expressed gratitude to bystanders who came to her rescue outside her Wangaratta electorate office. Haines is in a serious but stable condition after the alleged attack, which led to her losing both legs. A 43-year-old man has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. “Phil told us about your first words when you woke up after the attack,” Spender told parliament as she paid tribute to Haines. “Your first concerns when you awoke were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders. “That exactly speaks to the character of who you are. “People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition. But I think it paints a sort of picture of you as a sort of benign force wandering through the parliament. What I will say is that you are also a force for change.” ‘Like a stone in our hearts’ The prime minister, Anthony Albanese , led tributes on Monday. MPs wore baby’s breath flowers and orange heart lapel pins in the chamber. An orange cockatoo, synonymous with Haines’ local campaign, has been placed at her seat in the House of Representatives. Albanese called her “a fighter” and said the shock from the alleged attack was “like a stone in our hearts”. He urged politicians and voters not to shrug off the “very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”. “Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence.” Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The episode has created debate about the safety of MPs and the state of the political environment. But the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and the One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce have rejected calls for a change in parliamentary practice to cool Australia’s political debate. “In the past week, it has been suggested by some there is a causal connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence,” Taylor said. “I disagree with this view. “The Westminster system is about settling differences through robust and rigorous debate, not violence. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Haines tribute speeches to open parliament, but Labor mustn’t overlook broader causes of boiling anger | Josh Butler Read more “Importantly, we debate with adversarial vigour, but we never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence. People who resort to intimidation and violence cross a line that must never be crossed.” He said Labor had been right to call out far-right extremism in Australia but called for all extremism to be rejected. He said judges should “come down harder” on people found guilty of intimidation or violence. “Another thing we must do is celebrate Australia more readily. Too many Australians have been taught to feel guilty and shame about our country and about our history. 39:50 “Is it any wonder that some feel deep animosity towards our democracy, our institutions, and our nation?” Joyce told News24 his thoughts and prayers remained with Haines and her family, calling the alleged attack “so unAustralian”. “Unfortunately what we’re seeing in Australia and around the world is a change in dynamics,” Joyce said. “I think parliament has got its part to play but I don’t think its going to be a solution to the problem. “The issues, such as the Palestinian march across the [Sydney Harbour] Bridge, the vindictive, arsenic type of rhetoric that we see in the public realm, these are all part of it. “I think it’s foolish to think if question time changes, Australia changes. Not necessarily, in fact highly unlikely.” MPs are being encouraged to sign on to a civility pledge this week, promising to act with honesty, respect, and compassion. The speaker, Milton Dick, told parliament all MPs were thinking of Haines and praying for her recovery. “We look forward to the day you return to this place, and I get to say the following nine words: ‘I give the call to the member for Indi.’” Explore more on these topics Helen Haines Anthony Albanese Angus Taylor Barnaby Joyce Independents Coalition One Nation news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Live Australia politics live: Haines’s first words after waking were of concern for staff and bystanders; parliament hears emotional tributes to MP Unreasonable and unfair: damning investigation criticises Labor’s algorithm-based tool for aged care Haines tribute speeches to open parliament, but Labor mustn’t overlook broader causes of boiling anger AFP boss says politicians’ heated rhetoric is fuelling threats against MPs The tragic events of the past week have shown Australians who we are – and it’s a long way from our image of ourselves Helen Haines’s condition improves days after losing both legs from alleged attack The alleged attack on Helen Haines shocked the nation.
